This vignette explains *why* aidR is built the way it is. For a hands-on walkthrough, see `vignette("aidR")`; for platform-specific details, see the `format-*` vignettes.

## Goal: one interface, many platforms

Every AID platform exports the same underlying concepts (CGM readings, basal delivery, boluses, carbohydrate intake) but encodes them differently: different file layouts, column names, units, languages, and levels of detail. aidR's central design goal is that downstream analysis code should not need to know which platform a participant's data came from. Everything upstream of `parse_data(clean_files = TRUE)` is platform-specific; everything downstream works on a small, fixed set of standardized data frames.

## Detecting formats from content, not filenames

`parse_data()` never looks at a file's name or extension (beyond filtering out obviously irrelevant extensions like `.png`/`.pdf`/`.txt`) to decide which platform it came from. Instead, each platform has an `.is_<platform>_format.aidR()` function that inspects the file's actual structure:

- exact header match, for platforms with stable, English, machine-generated headers (YourLoops, Tandem Source);
- structural fingerprints, for platforms whose headers vary by account language (Glooko: first-line pattern + column count/type; mylife: number of dot-separated header fields);
- content markers, for single-file, multi-section platforms (CareLink: `-------` section separators; Tidepool: presence of a `"CGM"` sheet in the workbook).

This is why users can drop a folder containing exports from several participants and several platforms (even nested inside `.zip` archives) into `parse_data()` and have every file routed to the right parser automatically -- see `vignette("aidR")` for an example.


## Standardizing the core types, preserving the rest

Regardless of platform, when running `parse_data()` with `clean = TRUE`, a subset of five standardized data frames is produced:

- **`cgm`**: `id`, `format`, `timestamp`, `timezone_offset`, `value`, `unit` and `sensor_name`
- **`basal`**: `id`, `format`, `timestamp`, `timezone_offset`, `duration`, `rate`, `unit` and `pump_name`
- **`bolus`**: `id`, `format`, `timestamp`, `timezone_offset`, `type`, `total`, `normal`, `extended`, `unit`, `duration_extended` and `pump_name`
- **`carbs`**: `id`, `format`, `timestamp`, `timezone_offset`, `carbs`, `unit`, `label`, `estimated_absorption_duration`, and `is_hypo_treatment`
- **`SMBG`**: `id`, `format`, `timestamp`, `timezone_offset`, `value`, `unit` and `sensor_name`

Not every platform reports every core type (mylife, for example, only ever reports `bolus`, `carbs` and `SMBG`), and platforms routinely report additional information that has no equivalent elsewhere (CareLink's sensor calibrations and device-change events; Tidepool's pump-setting sheets; Glooko's exercise and medication logs). This information is still available when running `clean = FALSE` and can therefore be used for particular analyses requiring it.
